questions.stem: A cube-shaped cell has sides of 4 micrometres. What is its surface-area-to-volume ratio?
questions.explanation: Surface area = 6 x 4 x 4 = 96 square micrometres and volume = 4 x 4 x 4 = 64 cubic micrometres, so the ratio is 96/64 = 1.5 : 1. Dividing volume by area gives 0.67, and 6 : 1 is the ratio for a 1 micrometre cube.

questions.stem: As a spherical cell grows larger, what happens to its surface-area-to-volume ratio, and why does this matter?
options: It falls, so the cell takes up materials faster because there is more cytoplasm to fill
It falls, so the membrane can supply materials less fast than the cell's volume needs them
It rises, so the cell gains materials faster than it can use them and must stop growing
It stays the same, because the surface area and the volume both increase as the cell grows
questions.explanation: Surface area increases with the square of the radius but volume with the cube, so the ratio falls as a cell grows. The membrane then cannot exchange materials fast enough for the larger volume, which limits cell size.

questions.stem: Two cells have the same volume. One is a sphere; the other is long and flattened. Which statement about exchange across their membranes is correct, other factors being equal?
options: The flattened cell has the larger SA:V ratio, so materials reach its centre faster
The spherical cell has the larger SA:V ratio, because a sphere has the most surface
Both cells exchange materials at the same rate, because their volumes are identical
The flattened cell exchanges materials more slowly, because its membrane is stretched
questions.explanation: For a given volume, a sphere has the smallest possible surface area. Flattening or elongating a cell increases its surface area and shortens the distance to its centre, so exchange is faster.

questions.stem: Besides surface-area-to-volume ratio, which factor most increases the rate of diffusion of oxygen into a cell?
options: A larger volume of cytoplasm inside the cell's membrane
A lower temperature, which slows the movement of molecules
A steeper concentration gradient across the membrane
A thicker cell membrane with more phospholipid layers
questions.explanation: Diffusion is faster with a steeper concentration gradient, a larger surface and a shorter distance. A thicker membrane lengthens the distance, and lower temperature slows molecular movement.

questions.stem: Small, non-polar molecules such as oxygen cross the cell membrane easily, but glucose needs carrier proteins. Why?
options: Oxygen is a charged ion, so it is attracted through the membrane by its phosphate heads
Glucose dissolves in lipids, so it would become trapped inside the membrane's core
Glucose is larger and polar, so it cannot pass easily through the phospholipid bilayer
Glucose is smaller than oxygen, so it slips between the carrier proteins too quickly
questions.explanation: The hydrophobic core of the bilayer lets small non-polar molecules through but blocks larger polar molecules and ions, which need channel or carrier proteins. The physical and chemical nature of a substance is one of the factors affecting exchange.

questions.stem: A large animal has a much smaller SA:V ratio than a single cell. How do multicellular animals still supply every cell with oxygen?
options: Their cells need no oxygen, because they respire anaerobically to make all their ATP
Their cells are much larger, which increases the SA:V ratio of the whole organism
Large specialised exchange surfaces, and a circulatory system to carry gases
Every cell absorbs oxygen directly through the skin, which covers the entire body
questions.explanation: Diffusion alone is too slow over large distances, so animals have folded exchange surfaces such as alveoli and a transport system that brings blood close to every cell. Larger cells would lower, not raise, the SA:V ratio.

questions.stem: Which example is correctly matched to its level of organisation?
options: A leaf: an organ
Xylem: a cell
A root hair: a tissue
A stoma: an organ system
questions.explanation: A leaf is an organ made of several tissues, including epidermis, mesophyll, xylem and phloem. Xylem is a tissue, a root hair is part of a single cell, and a stoma is a pore between two guard cells.

questions.stem: The lungs, trachea, bronchi and diaphragm work together to move air and exchange gases. What does this group make up?
options: A single tissue
A single organ
A cell type
An organ system
questions.explanation: Several organs working together form an organ system, here the respiratory system. A tissue is a group of similar cells with one function, and an organ is made of several tissues.

questions.stem: What is cell specialisation?
options: The development of a cell's structure to suit it to a particular function
The division of one cell into two identical cells that both keep dividing
The loss of genes from a cell so that it can only carry out one function
The movement of a cell to a new tissue where its genes become activated
questions.explanation: As cells differentiate they develop features, such as shape, organelles and proteins, that suit a particular job. They keep their full set of genes; what changes is which genes are expressed.

questions.stem: A skin cell and a nerve cell from the same person contain the same DNA, yet they have very different structures. What explains this?
options: Each cell type loses the genes it does not need during development
Each cell type receives a different set of chromosomes from the parents
Mutations during mitosis give each cell type a different set of genes
Different genes are switched on in each cell type during differentiation
questions.explanation: Differentiation results from differential gene expression: each cell type transcribes a different subset of the same genome. Cells do not lose genes, and mitosis copies the DNA faithfully.

questions.stem: How is a mammalian red blood cell specialised for its function?
options: It has many chloroplasts, which make the oxygen it then transports
It lacks a nucleus, leaving more room for haemoglobin to carry oxygen
It has many mitochondria, which use the oxygen it carries for energy
It has a long axon, which carries signals rapidly around the body
questions.explanation: Mature red blood cells lose their nucleus and most organelles, so they are packed with haemoglobin, and their biconcave shape gives a large surface. They have no mitochondria, so they do not use the oxygen they carry.

questions.stem: Why do palisade mesophyll cells have many more chloroplasts than the cells of the lower epidermis?
options: They lie near the upper surface and are specialised for capturing light for photosynthesis
They lie near the lower surface and are specialised for controlling the opening of stomata
They are the only cells in a leaf that carry out respiration, which needs chloroplasts
They transport sugars to the rest of the plant, which needs energy from chloroplasts
questions.explanation: Palisade cells are tall, packed with chloroplasts and close to the upper surface where light is strongest, so they carry out most photosynthesis. Respiration happens in mitochondria in all living cells.

questions.stem: In mammals, where does gas exchange between air and blood take place?
options: Across the walls of the trachea
Across the walls of the bronchi
Across the lining of the mouth
Across the walls of the alveoli
questions.explanation: The alveoli are tiny air sacs at the ends of the bronchioles, surrounded by capillaries. The trachea and bronchi are airways that conduct air but are too thick-walled for exchange.

questions.stem: Which feature of the alveoli shortens the distance that oxygen must diffuse into the blood?
options: Their walls and the capillary walls are each only one cell thick
They are surrounded by rings of cartilage that hold them open
They are lined with cilia that sweep mucus away from the surface
They contain smooth muscle that pushes air into the capillaries
questions.explanation: Thin, flattened epithelial cells in the alveolus and the capillary give a very short diffusion path. Cartilage rings and cilia are features of the trachea and bronchi, not the alveoli.

questions.stem: Why is the inner surface of the alveoli kept moist?
options: Water molecules carry oxygen across the membrane by active transport
Oxygen must dissolve in the fluid lining before it can diffuse across the cells
Water reacts with carbon dioxide in the alveoli to release extra oxygen gas
Moisture adds weight that stops the alveoli from inflating too far in breathing
questions.explanation: Gases cross cell membranes in solution, so oxygen dissolves in the thin film of fluid before diffusing into the cells and blood. The fluid also contains surfactant, which stops the alveoli collapsing.

questions.stem: How do breathing and blood flow keep oxygen diffusing into the blood at the alveoli?
options: Breathing pushes oxygen through the alveolar walls by pressure, so no gradient is needed
Blood flow keeps the oxygen concentration in the capillaries higher than in the alveoli
Breathing removes carbon dioxide, which is the only gas that needs a concentration gradient
Breathing brings in fresh air and blood carries oxygen away, keeping the gradient steep
questions.explanation: Ventilation keeps alveolar oxygen high and continuous blood flow keeps capillary oxygen low, so a steep gradient is maintained. If capillary oxygen were higher than alveolar oxygen, oxygen would diffuse the wrong way.

questions.stem: In emphysema, the walls between alveoli break down, forming fewer, larger air spaces. Why does this make a person breathless?
options: The total surface area for gas exchange is reduced, so less oxygen enters the blood
The diffusion distance becomes shorter, so oxygen diffuses into the blood too quickly
The air spaces fill with blood, so oxygen cannot reach the walls of the alveoli
The alveoli become too small to hold air, so less air enters with each breath
questions.explanation: Many small alveoli provide a huge surface area; merging them into fewer large spaces reduces that area, so gas exchange falls. The spaces are larger, not smaller, and do not fill with blood.

questions.stem: In fish gills, blood in the lamellae flows in the opposite direction to the water passing over them. What is the advantage of this countercurrent flow?
options: Oxygen moves from the blood into the water, which removes oxygen the fish cannot use
A concentration gradient is kept along the whole lamella, so more oxygen is absorbed
The blood and water mix together, so oxygen moves directly into the red blood cells
Water flows more slowly over the gills, so the fish uses less energy to breathe
questions.explanation: Because blood always meets water with a higher oxygen concentration than itself, diffusion continues along the full length of the lamella. With parallel flow the two would reach equilibrium partway along, and less oxygen would be absorbed.

questions.stem: Insects have no lungs. How do their cells obtain oxygen?
options: Oxygen diffuses through the hard exoskeleton directly into every cell of the body
Air is pumped into the heart, which pushes it through blood vessels to the cells
Air travels through a network of tracheal tubes that reach close to the cells
Oxygen is carried from the gut to the cells by haemoglobin in the insect's blood
questions.explanation: Air enters through spiracles and moves along branching tracheae and fine tracheoles that deliver oxygen directly to the tissues. Insect blood plays little part in carrying oxygen, and the waxy exoskeleton limits diffusion through the surface.

questions.stem: Blood leaving the lungs has a high oxygen concentration. Which feature of capillaries lets this oxygen reach body cells quickly?
options: Their wide central space lets blood flow fast, so it spends little time in tissues
Their walls are a single layer of thin cells, close to the cells they supply
Their walls are thick and muscular, which squeezes oxygen out under pressure
Their valves prevent backflow, so blood moves through the tissues more quickly
questions.explanation: Capillary walls are one cell thick and capillaries run close to almost every cell, so the diffusion distance is short. Their narrow width also slows the blood, giving more time for exchange.

questions.stem: Carbon dioxide, oxygen and water vapour diffuse into and out of a leaf mainly through which structures?
options: Root hairs
Stomata
Xylem vessels
Phloem sieve tubes
questions.explanation: Stomata are pores, mostly in the leaf epidermis, through which carbon dioxide, oxygen and water vapour diffuse. Xylem and phloem transport water and sugars, not gases.

questions.stem: Once carbon dioxide enters a leaf, how does it reach the mesophyll cells?
options: By translocation in the phloem from the stomata to the cells
By active transport through the cell walls of the epidermis
By diffusion through the air spaces between the cells
By transport in the xylem from the stomata to the cells
questions.explanation: Gases move within the plant by diffusion through air spaces, especially in the spongy mesophyll. The course notes that this movement does not involve the plant's transport system.

questions.stem: How do the cells inside a woody stem, covered by bark, exchange gases with the air?
options: Through lenticels, small pores in the bark where cells are loosely packed
Through the xylem, which carries oxygen dissolved in water from the leaves
Through the phloem, which carries oxygen together with sugars from the leaves
Through the stomata of the leaves, which pump air down the stem to the cells
questions.explanation: Lenticels are areas of loosely packed cells in bark that allow gases to diffuse in and out. Plants exchange gases through stomata and their surface rather than carrying gases in xylem or phloem.

questions.stem: A leaf is kept in the dark overnight. Which describes its net gas exchange?
options: It exchanges no gases, because stomata stay fully closed in the dark
It takes in both gases equally, because respiration and photosynthesis balance
It takes in oxygen and releases carbon dioxide, because only respiration occurs
It takes in carbon dioxide and releases oxygen, because photosynthesis continues
questions.explanation: Without light there is no photosynthesis, but respiration continues, so the leaf uses oxygen and releases carbon dioxide. In bright light, photosynthesis is faster than respiration and the net exchange reverses.

questions.stem: What controls the opening and closing of stomata?
options: Xylem vessels that push the pore open when they fill with water
Changes in the water content of the two guard cells around each pore
Contraction of muscle fibres attached to the edges of each pore
The pressure of the carbon dioxide gas inside the leaf air spaces
questions.explanation: When guard cells take up water they swell and curve apart, opening the pore; when they lose water they become limp and the pore closes. Plants have no muscle tissue.

questions.stem: Which materials does the xylem of a flowering plant carry?
options: Water and mineral ions from the roots to the rest of the plant
Sugars from the leaves to the roots, fruits and growing tips
Oxygen and carbon dioxide between the leaves and the roots
Hormones and enzymes from the roots up to the flowers only
questions.explanation: Xylem carries water and dissolved minerals upward from the roots. Sugars and other products of photosynthesis move in the phloem, and gases move by diffusion through air spaces.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the transpiration stream?
options: Water rises in the xylem because it is lighter than the surrounding air
Evaporation from leaves pulls a column of water up the xylem
Water is pumped up the xylem by contractions of the living xylem cells
Sugars in the phloem draw water up from the roots by osmosis in the stem
questions.explanation: Water evaporating from mesophyll cells and diffusing out of stomata creates a tension that pulls water up the xylem. Xylem vessels are dead cells, so they cannot pump.

questions.stem: Why does the water column in the xylem not break as it is pulled up a tall tree?
options: Hydrogen bonds hold water molecules together, and water adheres to the xylem walls
Covalent bonds join water molecules end to end, forming a solid chain in the xylem
The xylem walls contract behind the water, pushing each section of the column upward
Air bubbles between water molecules hold the column up like a series of floats
questions.explanation: Cohesion between water molecules, due to hydrogen bonding, and adhesion to the lignified walls keep the column continuous under tension. Air bubbles would break the column, which is why embolisms block xylem.

questions.stem: A plant's stem is cut just above the soil and sap oozes from the cut stump, even though no leaves remain. What causes this?
options: Translocation: the phloem moves sugars upward, which carries water out of the cut
Cohesion: water molecules attract each other strongly enough to climb out unaided
Root pressure: ions taken up by roots draw in water, which is pushed up
Transpiration: evaporation from the stump pulls water up from the roots below
questions.explanation: Without leaves there is no transpiration pull, so the sap is being pushed from below. Roots load ions into the xylem, water follows by osmosis, and the resulting root pressure forces sap up and out.

questions.stem: Which change would most increase the rate of water movement up the xylem of a leafy plant?
options: Removing most of the leaves
A warm, dry, windy day
A cool, humid, still day
Closing all the stomata
questions.explanation: Warmth, low humidity and wind increase evaporation and diffusion of water vapour from leaves, strengthening the transpiration pull. Closing stomata or removing leaves reduces transpiration.

questions.stem: How is a xylem vessel suited to its function?
options: It is a layer of flattened cells covered with a thick waxy cuticle
It is a hollow tube of dead cells with lignified walls and no end walls
It is a column of living cells with sieve plates and companion cells
It is a single long cell filled with chloroplasts for making sugars
questions.explanation: Dead, empty xylem vessels form continuous tubes with little resistance to flow, and lignin strengthens them against collapse under tension. Sieve plates and companion cells are features of phloem.

questions.stem: Plant biologists use the term translocation. Which process does it describe?
options: The movement of water and mineral ions from the roots in the xylem
The loss of water vapour from leaves through stomata by evaporation
The movement of gases through the air spaces between mesophyll cells
The movement of sugars and other photosynthetic products in phloem
questions.explanation: Translocation moves sucrose, amino acids and some mineral nutrients through phloem sieve tubes. Water and minerals moving up the xylem form the transpiration stream.

questions.stem: In translocation, what is a sink?
options: A part of the plant where water is lost to the air, such as a stoma
A part of the plant where minerals are absorbed, such as a root hair
A part of the plant where sugars are used or stored, such as a root or fruit
A part of the plant where sugars are made, such as a mature leaf in light
questions.explanation: Phloem carries sugars from sources, where they are made or released from storage, to sinks, where they are used or stored. A storage organ can be a sink in summer and a source in spring.

questions.stem: Why can the phloem in one plant carry sap both up and down the stem, while xylem carries water only upward?
options: Phloem sap is lighter than water, so it can be pumped in any direction
Phloem is made of dead cells, so sap can flow through it either way
Phloem flows from sources to sinks, which can be above or below them
Phloem flows from the roots upward in the day and downward at night
questions.explanation: Sugars move towards whichever sinks are active, such as roots below or fruits and buds above, so flow direction varies between sieve tubes. Xylem flow is driven by transpiration from the leaves above, so it moves upward.

questions.stem: In the pressure-flow model of translocation, why does phloem sap move from a source to a sink?
options: Transpiration from the sink pulls sap through the phloem in the same way it pulls water in xylem
Companion cells beside the sieve tubes contract in waves, pumping the sap towards the sink
Sugar loaded at the source draws in water, building pressure that pushes sap to the sink
Sugar unloaded at the source leaves the sap dilute, so it is pulled towards the sink by tension
questions.explanation: Active loading of sucrose at the source lowers the water potential, water enters from the xylem by osmosis and hydrostatic pressure rises. Unloading at the sink lowers the pressure there, so sap flows from high to low pressure.

questions.stem: A ring of bark, including the phloem, is removed from around a tree trunk, leaving the xylem intact. After some weeks the bark just above the ring swells. Why?
options: Sugars moving down in the phloem build up above the ring, where flow is cut off
Water moving up in the xylem builds up above the ring, where it can no longer pass
Minerals from the roots collect above the ring, because the phloem carried them up
Gases trapped in the trunk collect above the ring, because the lenticels are removed
questions.explanation: Removing the phloem blocks the downward flow of sugars from the leaves, so they accumulate above the ring and the tissue there swells. The xylem is intact, so water still moves up and the leaves stay alive for a time.

questions.stem: Which cells keep phloem sieve tubes alive and help load sugars into them?
options: Guard cells
Xylem vessels
Root hair cells
Companion cells
questions.explanation: Sieve tube elements lose their nucleus and most organelles, so neighbouring companion cells supply proteins and ATP and help load sucrose. Guard cells control stomata.
